It is shown here only for its 13th-century phase.

column7: PH Chief court of the kings and princes of Gwynedd 600->1283 size=2 | Village; court dismantled 1283->None size=1
column9: SUM By tradition the chief seat of the kings of Gwynedd, on the west coast of Anglesey; the princes styled themselves ‘prince of Aberffraw’ in the 13th century. The settlement declined after a great storm in 1331 altered the coast.
column10: UNC Coflein reports the royal seat as tradition. The position of the llys within the village is not securely established and the start date is a placeholder; documentary references begin in the 7th-9th centuries.

column7: PH Late Roman and post-Roman stronghold 300->600 size=1 | No occupation known 600->1180 size=0 | Stone tower of the princes of Gwynedd 1180->1283 size=1 | Ruin 1283->None size=0
column9: SUM A rocky stronghold above Nant Gwynant, the legendary site of Vortigern’s fortress and Merlin’s dragons. Excavations in 1910 and 1954-6 found Iron Age, Roman and early medieval occupation; a stone tower was added at the end of the 12th century.
column10: UNC The phases of occupation are not closely dated and the years are placeholders. The Vortigern story is 9th-century legend.

column7: PH Royal crannog of Brycheiniog 890->916 size=2 | Burnt island 916->None size=0
column9: SUM The only crannog (artificial island) known in Wales, built in Llangorse Lake for the king of Brycheiniog from timbers felled between AD 889 and 893. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that a Mercian army sent by Æthelflæd destroyed ‘Brecenanmere’ in 916 and took the king’s wife captive.
column10: UNC The identification of ‘Brecenanmere’ with the crannog is probable, not certain.

column7: PH Post-Roman chieftain’s stronghold 450->700 size=1 | Abandoned 700->None size=0
column9: SUM A small defended hilltop near Cardiff, excavated by Leslie Alcock in the 1950s. Imported Mediterranean and Gaulish pottery, glass and fine metalworking show a wealthy household of the 5th to 7th centuries.
column10: UNC The dating of the ramparts has been revised more than once and the end date is approximate. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

column7: PH Inscribed memorial cross of the kings of Powys 825->None size=1
column9: SUM The shaft of a 9th-century cross near Llangollen, set up by Cyngen, king of Powys (died 854/5), in honour of his great-grandfather Eliseg. Its long Latin inscription, now illegible, traced the dynasty’s descent.
column10: UNC Cadw’s page dates the pillar only to the 9th century; the attribution to Cyngen depends on a transcript of the inscription made in 1696, and the year shown is a placeholder within his reign.

column7: PH Castle and borough at the Wye crossing 1067->None size=2
column9: SUM A castle on a cliff above the Wye, begun in 1067 by William fitz Osbern, earl of Hereford, and one of the first Norman strongholds in Wales. Its great tower is among the oldest stone castle buildings in Britain; a walled port town grew beside it.
column10: UNC Some scholars date the great tower to William I’s visit of 1081 or later, not to fitz Osbern.

column7: PH Earth-and-timber castle 1093->1200 size=1 | Stone castle and walled town 1200->None size=2
column9: SUM A castle on a tidal promontory, established by the Normans about 1093-4 and never taken by the Welsh. The round great tower was built at the start of the 13th century; Henry Tudor, later Henry VII, was born here in 1457.
column10: UNC Coflein gives ‘about 1094’ for the foundation. The link of the great tower with William Marshal and the birth of Henry VII are from general knowledge.

column7: PH Series of Roman forts 55->280 size=1 | Stone-walled Roman fort 280->380 size=2 | Empty fort walls 380->1081 size=0 | Norman castle and borough 1081->1300 size=2 | Chief town of Glamorgan 1300->None size=2
column9: SUM A series of Roman forts stood beside the Taff from the late 50s AD to the late 4th century. About 1081 William I set a castle inside the walls of the last fort, and the borough beside it became the head of the lordship of Glamorgan and one of the larger towns in Wales.
column10: UNC The date of the stone fort (late 3rd century) and the size of the medieval town are from general knowledge; the Roman name is uncertain (Pleiades offers ‘Tamion?’). Nothing is known of the site between the 4th and 11th centuries.

column7: PH Concentric castle with water defences 1268->1500 size=2 | Castle in decay 1500->None size=1
column9: SUM The largest castle in Wales, begun in 1268 by Gilbert de Clare, lord of Glamorgan, against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. Its concentric walls and wide artificial lakes were new to Britain.
column10: UNC The date by which the castle was ruinous is approximate (it was derelict when John Leland saw it in the 1530s).

column7: PH Castle of the princes of Gwynedd 1210->1283 size=1 | English garrison 1283->1300 size=1 | Little used 1300->None size=0
column9: SUM A stone keep guarding a route through Snowdonia, built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, ruler of Gwynedd from 1201 to 1240. It fell to Edward I in 1283, who refitted it.
column10: UNC The building date is not recorded; 1210 is a placeholder within Llywelyn’s reign. The castle was lived in again from the late 15th century, which is not shown.

column7: PH Castle of the princes of Gwynedd, then English 1221->1294 size=1 | Abandoned 1294->None size=0
column9: SUM A castle on a rock in the Dysynni valley, begun in 1221 by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth to guard the southern border of Gwynedd. It was taken by Edward I’s forces in 1283 and given up after the Welsh rising of 1294.
column10: UNC

column7: PH Castle of the princes of Gwynedd 1210->1284 size=1 | Abandoned tower 1284->None size=0
column9: SUM A round stone tower at the foot of the Llanberis pass, most likely built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth in the late 12th or early 13th century.
column10: UNC Cadw gives only ‘late 12th or early 13th century’; 1210 is a placeholder. The end date reflects the removal of its timber to Caernarfon in 1284, a detail from general knowledge.

column7: PH Castle of the princes of Gwynedd 1230->1283 size=1 | English castle and borough 1283->1404 size=1 | Burnt ruin 1404->None size=0
column9: SUM A castle on a headland in Cardigan Bay. Llywelyn ap Iorwerth built the twin-towered gatehouse, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd added the outer ward, Edward I refitted it, and Owain Glyndŵr burnt it in 1404.
column10: UNC The first building date is not recorded; about 1230 is the usual estimate, from general knowledge.

column7: PH Edward I’s castle and borough 1277->None size=2
column9: SUM The first of Edward I’s castles in Wales, begun in 1277 and largely finished by 1284, with a planned borough beside it. Richard II met Henry Bolingbroke here in 1399.
column10: UNC

column7: PH English burh, then Welsh royal seat 921->1063 size=1 | Norman motte and borough 1073->1277 size=1 | Edward I’s castle and borough 1277->None size=2
column9: SUM The lowest crossing of the Clwyd. Edward the Elder founded a burh here in 921; it was Gruffudd ap Llywelyn’s seat until 1063; Robert of Rhuddlan raised a motte in 1073. Edward I began the present concentric castle in 1277 and issued the Statute of Rhuddlan here in 1284.
column10: UNC Only the 1277 date comes from Cadw and the Statute from the Bodleian guide. The burh of ‘Cledemutha’ (921), Gruffudd’s court and the motte of 1073 are from general knowledge; the identification of Cledemutha with Rhuddlan is generally, not universally, accepted.

column7: PH Aberconwy Abbey 1186->1283 size=1 | Edward I’s castle and walled town 1283->None size=2
column9: SUM Edward I and Master James of St George built the castle and a 1.3 km circuit of town walls here between 1283 and 1287. The site had been the Cistercian abbey of Aberconwy, burial place of Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, which the king moved up the valley to Maenan.
column10: UNC The abbey phase (founded 1186, on this site from the 1190s) is from general knowledge.

column7: PH Norman motte 1090->1115 size=1 | Court of the princes of Gwynedd 1115->1283 size=1 | Edward I’s castle and walled borough; seat of government for North Wales 1283->1536 size=3 | County town; castle in decay 1536->None size=2
column9: SUM Edward I began the castle and walled borough in 1283, with a quay, all at once; work lasted 47 years and was still unfinished about 1330. It was the centre of royal government in North Wales. The castle was in decay by the 16th century.
column10: UNC The Norman motte of about 1090 and the Welsh court that followed are from general knowledge and their dates are approximate.

column7: PH Edward I’s castle 1283->1404 size=2 | Court of Owain Glyndŵr 1404->1409 size=2 | Royal castle 1409->None size=1
column9: SUM A concentric castle on a crag above Cardigan Bay, begun in May 1283 and largely complete by 1289. Owain Glyndŵr took it in 1404 and kept his court and family here until it was retaken in 1409; it fell again to the Yorkists in 1468 after a long siege.
column10: UNC

column7: PH Edward I’s unfinished castle; borough and port 1295->None size=2
column9: SUM The last of Edward I’s Welsh castles, begun in 1295 after the rising of Madog ap Llywelyn. Money ran short and work petered out by the 1320s, leaving the towers below their planned height. The borough became the main port of Anglesey.
column10: UNC Glyndŵr’s supporters held it from 1403 for about two years, which is not shown as a phase.

column7: PH Norman castle and borough 1106->None size=1
column9: SUM A Norman ringwork of the early 12th century, rebuilt in stone as a concentric castle in the late 13th and 14th centuries. The Lord Rhys captured it in 1159.
column10: UNC Cadw gives only ‘early 12th century’; 1106 (the grant to Bishop Roger of Salisbury) is from general knowledge.

column7: PH Hen Domen, earth-and-timber castle 1071->1223 size=1 | Royal stone castle and borough 1223->None size=2
column9: SUM Henry III began the stone castle about 1223 against Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, replacing the nearby timber castle of Hen Domen. It withstood attacks in 1228, 1231 and 1245. The treaty that recognised Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales was sealed at the nearby ford in 1267.
column10: UNC The marker is at the stone castle; Hen Domen lies about 1.5 km north-west. Its foundation about 1071 by Roger of Montgomery is from general knowledge.

column7: PH Castle of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd 1273->1277 size=1 | Mortimer castle 1277->1390 size=1 | Abandoned 1390->None size=0
column9: SUM A castle built by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1273 on a ridge above the Severn, in defiance of the king and facing royal Montgomery. Roger Mortimer took it in 1277 after a two-week siege.
column10: UNC Cadw says only that it was abandoned in the 14th century; the end year is a placeholder.

column7: PH Fortress-palace of the Herberts and Somersets 1435->None size=2
column9: SUM A late medieval fortress-palace in Gwent. Sir William ap Thomas built the moated Great Tower about 1435 and his son William Herbert, earl of Pembroke, enlarged it.
column10: UNC An earlier manor stood here; it is not shown.

column7: PH Court of Dafydd ap Gruffudd 1260->1282 size=1 | De Lacy castle and walled borough 1282->None size=2
column9: SUM A Welsh princely residence of Dafydd ap Gruffudd, whose attack on Hawarden in 1282 set off Edward I’s final war. Henry de Lacy then built a large castle and walled town on the site; the half-built castle was captured in the rising of 1294.
column10: UNC The start date of the Welsh court is a placeholder. The position is from general knowledge.

column7: PH Hall of Owain Glyndŵr 1350->1403 size=1 | Burnt motte 1403->None size=0
column9: SUM A motte and bailey in the Cynllaith valley, the chief home of Owain Glyndŵr. A poem of about 1390 praises its fine timber hall on a green mound; it was burnt in 1403 and has no later history.
column10: UNC Coflein says the castle may be as early as the 12th century but direct evidence is lacking; the start date here marks only the 14th-century hall.

column7: PH Castle of the princes of Powys Fadog 1260->1277 size=1 | Burnt ruin 1277->None size=0
column9: SUM A hilltop castle above Llangollen, built inside an Iron Age hillfort by the rulers of northern Powys in the 1260s and burnt by its own garrison before Edward I’s army in 1277.
column10: UNC The building date is an estimate. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

column7: PH Cistercian abbey 1131->1536 size=2 | Roofless ruin 1536->None size=1
column9: SUM The first Cistercian abbey in Wales, founded in 1131 on the Wye. The great church was begun in 1269. The abbey surrendered in 1536 in the first round of the dissolution.
column10: UNC

column7: PH Cistercian abbey 1164->1539 size=2 | Ruin 1539->None size=0
column9: SUM A Cistercian abbey in the Ceredigion uplands, founded in 1164 by a Norman lord and soon taken under the patronage of the Lord Rhys. The monks entered their new church in 1201. Welsh princes were buried here and it supported the Welsh cause; it closed by 1539.
column10: UNC The first community may have begun on a different site nearby before moving here in the 1180s; the marker is at the later abbey.

column7: PH Cistercian abbey 1201->1537 size=1 | Ruin 1537->None size=0
column9: SUM A Cistercian abbey near Llangollen, founded in 1201 by Madog ap Gruffudd, prince of northern Powys, and named after the nearby Pillar of Eliseg. It was dissolved in 1537.
column10: UNC

column7: PH Abbey (Savigniac, then Cistercian) 1130->1539 size=2 | Ruin and mansion 1539->None size=0
column9: SUM Founded in 1130 by the Norman knight Richard de Granville; by the late 13th century one of the wealthiest abbeys in Wales.
column10: UNC The dissolution year (1539) and the abbey’s first affiliation to Savigny are from general knowledge; Cadw’s page gives neither.

column7: PH Cistercian abbey 1147->1536 size=2 | Nave kept as parish church 1536->None size=1
column9: SUM A Cistercian abbey founded about 1147 and dissolved in 1536, thought to stand on an earlier monastic site: early Christian carved stones were found around it. The western part of the nave survives as the parish church.
column10: UNC

column7: PH Abbey (Savigniac, then Cistercian) 1131->1536 size=1 | Ruin 1536->None size=0
column9: SUM An abbey near Holywell on the Dee estuary, founded in 1131 and much rebuilt in the 13th century. Wat’s Dyke reaches the estuary close by.
column10: UNC The dissolution year is from general knowledge. The first community may have been at a different site nearby.

column7: PH Norman castle and borough of Gower 1106->1300 size=1 | Port and market town 1300->None size=2
column9: SUM The castle at the mouth of the Tawe was founded in or soon after 1106 as the head of the Norman lordship of Gower; a borough and port grew beside it. The first castle was earth and timber, rebuilt in stone probably between 1221 and 1284.
column10: UNC Size is a rough judgement; medieval Swansea had perhaps 1,000-2,000 people. A Norse origin for the name is often suggested but no Viking-age settlement has been found.

column7: PH Castle and Flemish borough 1110->1300 size=1 | Chief town of Pembrokeshire 1300->None size=2
column9: SUM A castle founded about 1110 by Tancred, a Fleming, at the tidal limit of the Western Cleddau. The town below it became one of the largest and richest in medieval Wales.
column10: UNC The town’s later size is from general knowledge; it was made a county in itself in the late 15th or 16th century.

column7: PH Norman castle, priory and walled town 1093->None size=2
column9: SUM Bernard de Neufmarché defeated the king of Brycheiniog near here in 1093 and built a castle and a Benedictine priory (now the cathedral) at the meeting of the Usk and Honddu. A walled town followed.
column10: UNC The marker is at the priory church. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

column7: PH Market settlement in the lordship of Bromfield 1161->1400 size=1 | Largest town of north-east Wales 1400->None size=2
column9: SUM A market town on the Welsh side of the border, first recorded in the 12th century. It was never a chartered walled borough but by the 16th century was among the most populous towns in Wales.
column10: UNC The first mention (a castle at ‘Wristlesham’, 1161) and the growth of the town are from general knowledge; the phase dates are approximate.

column7: PH Edward I’s castle and borough 1277->None size=1
column9: SUM Edward I’s brother Edmund began the castle and borough in 1277, at first called Llanbadarn. Owain Glyndŵr held it from 1404 to 1408.
column10: UNC An earlier castle of the same name stood about 2 km to the south. The Dictionary of Welsh Biography confirms Glyndŵr’s capture of Aberystwyth in 1404; the other dates are from general knowledge.

column7: PH Norman castle, priory and town 1068->None size=1
column9: SUM William fitz Osbern built a castle where the Monnow meets the Wye soon after 1066; a priory and walled town followed. Henry V was born in the castle in 1386 or 1387. A Roman fort, Blestium, had stood here.
column10: UNC The Roman fort is not shown as a phase. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

column7: PH Market town 1291->None size=1
column9: SUM A small market town in the Dyfi valley, with a market charter of 1291. By tradition Owain Glyndŵr was crowned Prince of Wales and held a parliament here in 1404.
column10: UNC The 1404 parliament rests on later tradition and a few contemporary references; the ‘Parliament House’ shown in the town is a later building. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.
